title: Weak Legs and Saddle Sensory Loss / Identify New Cauda Equina Deterioration

blocks.text: Weak Legs and Saddle Sensory Loss / Identify New Cauda Equina Deterioration

Code R5-123 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examining; at least 4 questioning) · UK hospital outpatient setting · Source dates listed in §15 · AMaC examiner-style educational station; not an official PACES marking scheme.
Please examine this patient’s lower limbs to assess the cause and functional consequences of their weakness. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Chronic cauda equina damage produces bilateral lower motor neurone deficits and sphincter sequelae. The immediate safety question is whether anything has changed from baseline.

The Examiner Trap. Treating all longstanding bladder dysfunction as a new acute syndrome leads to imprecise presentation; conversely, dismissing new retention or saddle symptoms because there is an old diagnosis is dangerous.

blocks.text: Not applicable — this is an examination encounter with a patient, not a communication or consultation role-player. The patient may answer brief, natural questions but is not a surrogate.
Patient setup: A 49-year-old with longstanding bilateral leg weakness following a previous lumbar disc prolapse.
Finding-release protocol: do not announce a sign before the corresponding manoeuvre is performed.
Bilateral lower motor neurone weakness, most pronounced at ankles; reduced tone and diminished knee and ankle reflexes.
Patchy bilateral leg sensory loss; patient reports previous saddle numbness and neurogenic bladder managed by continence services.
No pyramidal signs. No new pain, weakness or sphincter change in the baseline scenario.
Normal-findings variant: Lower-limb findings may be subtle in a longstanding lesion; avoid inventing acute retention or new saddle loss.
Examiner question ladder (4–6 questions; 4-minute discussion):
Q1 [R2]: Where is the lesion?  Model: Multiple lumbosacral roots in the cauda equina; lower motor neurone signs rather than a thoracic cord syndrome.
Q2 [R3]: What tells you it is newly urgent?  Model: New urinary retention or altered urinary sensation, saddle sensory loss, bowel or sexual dysfunction, new bilateral weakness.
Q3 [R4]: What if the patient reports new bladder symptoms today?  Model: Emergency referral and urgent MRI through the suspected CES pathway; do not rely on a reassuring bedside residual volume.
Q4 [R5]: How do you manage chronic sequelae?  Model: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation plus bladder, bowel, pain, skin and mobility review.
Q5 [R6]: Which tests are useful?  Model: MRI for new compression; tailored bladder assessment and review of earlier imaging for established deficits.

Curveball: The candidate states a diagnosis with certainty before discussing alternatives. Safe response: “These are findings and a leading differential; confirmation needs the appropriate investigation.”
[R1; Skill A] Test segmental power, tone, reflexes, sensation and walking aid.
[R2; Skill B] Describe bilateral LMN pattern and sensory deficits.
[R3; Skill D] Localise the lesion to lumbosacral roots/cauda equina.
[R4; Skill E] Ask explicitly about new retention, incontinence, saddle sensory change and worsening weakness.
[R5; Skill E] Emergency MRI if new CES features; otherwise review existing imaging and rehabilitation needs.
[R6; Skill G] Seek consent for sensory testing and maintain dignity when discussing sphincter symptoms.
[G] Gains consent, checks discomfort, and protects dignity during examination.
Fail performance (AMaC educational illustration; not a literal examination outcome).
CANDIDATE: “I will have a quick look.” [R1 Fail]
EXAMINER: “What did you find?”
CANDIDATE: “It is probably chronic cauda equina lesion.” [R2 Fail; R3 Fail]
EXAMINER: “What happens next?”
CANDIDATE: “I would just follow up routinely.” [R4 Fail; R5 Fail]
Examiner note: The diagnosis is asserted without a supporting sign sequence, an alternative or a safe plan; patient comfort is not established. [R6 Fail]
Pass performance (minimum safe actions performed).
CANDIDATE: “Hello. I would like to examine you to help work out what is going on. Is that okay? Tell me if anything is painful.” [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: “Test segmental power, tone, reflexes, sensation and walking aid. I will do this systematically and help you if you are unsteady.” [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: “Summarise the key examination findings.”

CANDIDATE: “Bilateral lower motor neurone weakness, most pronounced at ankles; reduced tone and diminished knee and ankle reflexes. Patchy bilateral leg sensory loss; patient reports previous saddle numbness and neurogenic bladder managed by continence services.” [R2 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What is your impression?”
CANDIDATE: “Multiple lumbosacral roots in the cauda equina; lower motor neurone signs rather than a thoracic cord syndrome. I would also consider relevant alternatives.” [R3 Pass]
EXAMINER: “What would you do next?”

CANDIDATE: “Ask explicitly about new retention, incontinence, saddle sensory change and worsening weakness. Emergency MRI if new CES features; otherwise review existing imaging and rehabilitation needs.” [R4 Pass; R5 Pass]
Examiner note: Demonstrates a safe, adequately justified assessment and explicit welfare action.
High-performance performance (adds prioritisation and anticipatory reasoning).
CANDIDATE: “Before examining, I will check whether any manoeuvre worsens pain or threatens balance and maintain your privacy.” [R6 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “Screen for a sensory level and document residual deficits precisely.” [R1 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “Which signs are discriminating?”
CANDIDATE: “Avoid describing absent pyramidal signs as evidence against cauda equina. I will state clearly what I did not find.” [R2 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “What else could explain them?”
CANDIDATE: “Differentiate from cord compression, peripheral neuropathy and plexopathy.” [R3 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “How does that change your plan?”
CANDIDATE: “Compare with prior function; initiate emergency CES pathway if changes are new; plan spinal, urology, continence, bowel and mobility follow-up.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “I will document function and arrange appropriate assistance before the patient leaves.” [R6 High-performance]
Examiner note: Uses objective localisation, offers proportionate investigations, anticipates welfare concerns and avoids unjustified certainty.
R1 — Lower-limb examination: Failing to test segmental power, tone, reflexes, sensation and walking aid makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R2 — Identify objective signs: Failing to describe bilateral LMN pattern and sensory deficits makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R3 — Localisation: Failing to localise the lesion to lumbosacral roots/cauda equina makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R4 — Bladder and red flags: Failing to ask explicitly about new retention, incontinence, saddle sensory change and worsening weakness makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
“I need the baseline bladder and saddle function before calling this an acute change.”
“New neurological or bladder deterioration requires the emergency cauda equina pathway.”
Chronic cauda equina damage produces bilateral lower motor neurone deficits and sphincter sequelae. The immediate safety question is whether anything has changed from baseline.

Treating all longstanding bladder dysfunction as a new acute syndrome leads to imprecise presentation; conversely, dismissing new retention or saddle symptoms because there is an old diagnosis is dangerous.
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation plus bladder, bowel, pain, skin and mobility review.
THINK: new retention, saddle sensory change or weakness.
SAY: “Bilateral lumbosacral lower motor neurone findings.”
DO: define baseline; examine roots; screen new red flags.
NUMBERS: GIRFT suspected CES pathway (2023) specifies emergency assessment and MRI.
TRAP: “It has always been like that” without verifying change.
FINISH: emergency assessment if new; MDT rehabilitation if stable.

Educational use only. No automatic claim of examination scoring or independent clinical sign-off.

Even in an established chronic lesion, new bladder/bowel/sexual dysfunction, new saddle numbness or rapidly progressive weakness requires immediate referral via local cauda equina pathway. Do not assume all symptoms are chronic; emergency MRI and spinal assessment may be necessary. Document baseline versus change.
